archival_memory.user_gym_friends: I have some pretty good friends from the gym. Working out has always been an escape for me, and over time, I kept seeing the same group of people in the early mornings. It kind of turned into this friendly circle. One of those guys, Dean, is a fellow computer science major, but he's more into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. We started talking shop between sets, which led to us comparing notes on our classes, which then led to us being gym buddies who share nutritional tips, workout regimens—pretty much everything. Now, every so often, we'll game together, too. He's the one who got me hooked on a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's become a friendship built around mutual support—pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
archival_memory.user_gaming_friends: I have another circle of friends that's quite dear to me - the gaming group. I'm not a hardcore gamer, but I do spend a decent chunk of time on weekends playing multiplayer strategy games, especially when I need a mental break from writing code or reading research papers. We have this informal e-sports club that meets in a common lounge in our student center. I don't always go, but whenever I do, it's guaranteed quality time with friends. There's something special about gaming with a group in the same room - plenty of laughs, random inside jokes, that collective groan when a team fight goes south, and the ultimate hype when we pull off a last-second victory. Actually, I made a great friend, Derek, through that group - he's super skilled in networking security, and he taught me a bunch of techniques that later proved useful in a cybersecurity research project. And the best part is how naturally our friendship evolved - initially from a shared hobby, and later we just kept supporting each other academically.

archival_memory.user_library_friends: I have made some unexpected friendships in the campus library. As a fourth-year CS major, I spend a fair amount of time there when I want a quieter space to study. Over the years, I've bumped into the same faces in the same corner desks. One of those people is Jackson, a law student who somehow ended up reading case studies right next to my stack of cryptography textbooks. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. Over time, we realized we shared an interest in debates - oddly enough, he loves analyzing political and ethical implications of new technologies, so I'd talk to him all day about algorithmic bias. We discovered that, even though we come from different disciplines, we both care about how technology intersects with society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.

archival_memory.user_everyday_friends: I have made great friends in unexpected, everyday-life situations. There was this one day when I was super stressed with a research deadline. I was up too late the night before, so I rushed to the campus cafe half-asleep, waiting in a long line. I started complaining - under my breath, but loud enough for the person behind me to hear - about how I needed more time for my research code to run. Turns out, she was also in the thick of her own mechanical engineering lab fiasco. We commiserated, shared a laugh, and ended up sitting together for coffee. That day, we bonded so much over academic stress that we exchanged contact info, and now, whenever we see each other on campus, we make a point to catch up. She might not be a 'best friend' in the sense of constant hangouts, but it's still a positive, supportive relationship that started organically.

archival_memory.user_mutual_respect: What unites all these friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're all navigating this crazy journey together. Sometimes, people have this caricature of computer science majors as being antisocial or always stuck behind a screen, but truthfully, my experience has been the opposite. We form these deep connections, especially because the workload and pressure can be so high at times. We're in labs critiquing each other's code, or we're on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to some bug—and those challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.

archival_memory.user_graduation: As a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and that means a lot of goodbyes eventually. I'm excited about the future - internships, job prospects, maybe grad school. But I can't lie: I'm also dreading the day when all these friends I've made scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.

archival_memory.user_friendship_transcends_distance: I think that's what real friendship is: you may not always be geographically close, but you have this strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I learned that from Tony, who's interning across the country this semester, yet we still FaceTime regularly. I see the same dedication in others as well - like Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised that if either of us ends up in Europe, the other has to come visit.

archival_memory.user_friends_mean_everything: I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, random campus encounters - everything. They're truly an integral part of my college experience, and they remind me that there's more to this journey than racking up achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends... that's what success really looks like to me. And I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story - they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
